fr:mainmatter.html:p: Metatheoretic proofs often follow a common structure

html:ul.html:li: Construct a semantic domain encoding the desired property
Show it is a model of the syntax
Interpret the syntax in the model then read off the proof

html:div.html:p: Choice of language and semantic domain may vary, but the overall architecture is static across applications

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A library written in Cubical Agda for writing compositional metatheoretic proofs

html:div.html:p: The goal is not to develop a body of formalized category theory...but, category theory is conveniently well-suited to our needs, so we develop quite a bit

html:div.html:div: Compositonal construction of logical relations for simply typed \lambda -calculi

html:ul.html:li: Uses the language of displayed category theory
Extension of agda/cubical, the Cubical Agda standard library. Results occasionally merged upstream
Make heavy use of function extensionality, but minimal use of univalence
Nearly all of the code is --safe, except for a few experimental modules for guarded type theory

html:div.html:p: Define a predicate \llbracket {A}\rrbracket _{\mathsf {Canonical}} on closed terms for each type A, then show that all closed terms inhabit the predicate

html:div.style: border-left: 4px solid var(--accent); background: var(--bg-subtle, rgba(0,0,0,0.03)); padding: 0.7em 1em; margin: 0.8em 0; border-radius: 2px
color: var(--accent); font-variant: small-caps; letter-spacing: 0.12em; font-size: 0.85em; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.3em
text-align: center

html:div.html:p:
Think of the canonicity predicate as a dependent type
\llbracket {A}\rrbracket _{\mathsf {Canonical}} : {\mathopen {}\left (\cdot \vdash M : A\right )\mathclose {}} \to \mathbf {Type}

A proof of the fundamental theorem is then a dependent function, \mathsf {canonicity} : {\mathopen {}\left (\cdot \vdash M : A\right )\mathclose {}} \to \llbracket {A}\rrbracket _{\mathsf {Canonical}}M
Other logical relations take the same shape: proofs living over syntactic terms

html:div.style: border-left: 4px solid var(--accent); background: var(--bg-subtle, rgba(0,0,0,0.03)); padding: 0.7em 1em; margin: 0.8em 0; border-radius: 2px

html:div.html:div: How should we categorify this observation?

html:div.style: display: flex; gap: 2em; align-items: flex-start
flex: 5; min-width: 0
html:div.html:p: A displayed category \overline {\mathcal {D}} over \mathcal {C} assigns to each object x \in \mathcal {C} a family of objects \overline {\mathcal {D}}_{x} over x, and to each morphism f : x \to y, \overline {x} \in \overline {\mathcal {D}}_{x}, \overline {y} \in \overline {\mathcal {D}}_{y}, a family of morphisms \overline {\mathcal {D}}_{f}{\mathopen {}\left [\overline {x} , \overline {y}\right ]\mathclose {}} over f
It is a category varying over \mathcal {C}

html:div.style: flex: 3; min-width: 0
border-left: 4px solid var(--accent); background: var(--bg-subtle, rgba(0,0,0,0.03)); padding: 0.7em 1em; margin: 0.8em 0; border-radius: 2px

html:div.html:div: A category is to a context as a displayed category is to a dependent type

html:div.html:p: A section of \overline {\mathcal {D}} picks, for each x \in \mathcal {C}, an object s(x) over x, and for each f : x \to y a morphism s(f) : s(x) \to s(y) over f --- functorially

color: var(--accent); font-variant: small-caps; letter-spacing: 0.12em; font-size: 0.85em; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.3em

html:div.html:div: \mathbf {Syntax}_{\Sigma ,\times } is the free cartesian category over \Sigma : for every displayed cartesian category over it interpreting \Sigma , there exists a unique section.

html:div.html:div: What does it mean for \llbracket {-}\rrbracket _{\mathsf {Canonical}} to be a displayed cartesian category?

html:pre.html:code: record BinProduct (C : Category ℓ ℓ') (x y : C.ob) : Type (ℓ-max ℓ ℓ') where field binProdOb : C.ob binProdPr₁ : C.Hom[ binProdOb , x ] binProdPr₂ : C.Hom[ binProdOb , y ] univProp : isBinProduct binProdPr₁ binProdPr₂

html:div.html:p: Need individual definitons for Terminal, BinCoproduct, Exponential, etc
In cubical-categorical-logic, we give a uniform interface to universal properties

For a presheaf P : \mathsf {Psh}\,\mathcal {C} and object c \in \mathcal {C}, an element x \in P\,c determines a natural transformation \mathsf {rec}_{よ} {\mathopen {}\left (x\right )\mathclose {}} : よ\,c \Rightarrow P by the Yoneda Lemma. Call x a universal element when \mathsf {rec}_{よ} {\mathopen {}\left (x\right )\mathclose {}} is a natural isomorphism.

html:pre.html:code: record UniversalElement (C : Category ℓo ℓh) (P : Presheaf C ℓp) : Type (ℓ-max (ℓ-max ℓo ℓh) ℓp) where field vertex : C.ob element : (P ⟅ vertex ⟆) .fst universal : isUniversal vertex element

html:div.html:p: A product for x and y is then just a universal element for よ x \times よ y

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Most concepts in category theory port over directly to displayed categories
Given a presheaf P : \mathsf {Psh}\,\mathcal {C}, and \overline {\mathcal {D}} a displayed category over \mathcal {C}, we define displayed presheaves on \overline {\mathcal {D}} over P

html:div.html:p: Define \overline {\mathcal {D}} / P to be the (ordinary) category \int _{\mathcal {C}} {\mathopen {}\left (\overline {\mathcal {D}} \times \mathsf {Element}{\mathopen {}\left (P\right )\mathclose {}}\right )\mathclose {}}

html:ul.html:li: Objects are triples {\mathopen {}\left (c \in \mathcal {C} , \overline {c} \in \overline {\mathcal {D}}_{c} , x \in P\,c\right )\mathclose {}}

Morphisms from {\mathopen {}\left (c , \overline {c} , x\right )\mathclose {}} to {\mathopen {}\left (d , \overline {d} , y\right )\mathclose {}} are triples {\mathopen {}\left (f : c \to d , \overline {f} : \overline {\mathcal {D}}_{f}{\mathopen {}\left [\overline {c} , \overline {d}\right ]\mathclose {}} , {\mathopen {}\left (Pf\right )\mathclose {}}y = x\right )\mathclose {}}

html:div.html:p: A displayed presheaf \overline {P} over P is a presheaf on \overline {\mathcal {D}} / P. Write \overline {P} : \overline {\mathsf {Psh}}_{P}\,\overline {\mathcal {D}}. Intuitively, we can think of this like a presheaf on \int _{\mathcal {C}} \overline {\mathcal {D}} additionally parametrized by an element of P.

There are correspondening notions of displayed natural transformations of displayed presheafs, a displayed Yoneda embedding, etc
\overline {よ} \overline {c} = \overline {\mathcal {D}}_{-}{\mathopen {}\left [- , \overline {c}\right ]\mathclose {}} : \overline {\mathsf {Psh}}_{よ\,c}\,\overline {\mathcal {D}}
\overline {\mathcal {D}} is displayed cartesian when it has displayed products and a displayed terminal object
Let P : \mathsf {Psh}\,\mathcal {C}, \overline {\mathcal {D}} displayed over \mathcal {C}, and \overline {P} : \overline {\mathsf {Psh}}_{P}\,\overline {\mathcal {D}}

html:div.style: border-left: 4px solid var(--accent); background: var(--bg-subtle, rgba(0,0,0,0.03)); padding: 0.7em 1em; margin: 0.8em 0; border-radius: 2px
color: var(--accent); font-variant: small-caps; letter-spacing: 0.12em; font-size: 0.85em; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.3em

html:div.html:p: Say that \overline {x} is a displayed universal element when \mathsf {rec}_{よ} {\mathopen {}\left (x\right )\mathclose {}} is a natural isomorphism and \mathsf {rec}_{\overline {よ}} {\mathopen {}\left (\overline {x}\right )\mathclose {}} is a natural isomorphism over it

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Related to displayed universal elements are vertical universal elements

html:div.html:p: When \overline {P} is displayed over a representable よ x, call it a vertical presheaf
Then we characterize vertical universal elements \overline {x} \in \overline {P} {\mathopen {}\left (c , \overline {c} , \mathsf {id}\right )\mathclose {}} as before
When \overline {\mathcal {D}} has enough fibrational structure, usually one can construct displayed universal elements from corresponding vertical universal elements

html:div.style: border-left: 4px solid var(--accent); background: var(--bg-subtle, rgba(0,0,0,0.03)); padding: 0.7em 1em; margin: 0.8em 0; border-radius: 2px
color: var(--accent); font-variant: small-caps; letter-spacing: 0.12em; font-size: 0.85em; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.3em

html:div.html:div: If \overline {D} is a fibration and has all vertical binary products, then \overline {D} has all displayed binary products

html:div.style: border-left: 4px solid var(--accent); background: var(--bg-subtle, rgba(0,0,0,0.03)); padding: 0.7em 1em; margin: 0.8em 0; border-radius: 2px
color: var(--accent); font-variant: small-caps; letter-spacing: 0.12em; font-size: 0.85em; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.3em

html:div.html:div: To the keen-eyed, vertical universal elements look to be a special case of displayed universal elements. Morally they are, but technically they aren't unless the base category is strict. In particular, f \star \mathsf {id} = f definitionally in \mathcal {C}

html:div.style: display: flex; gap: 2em; align-items: flex-start
flex: 1; min-width: 0
html:div.html:p: Intuitively, the fiber over b \in \mathcal {B} is just the fiber of \overline {\mathcal {D}} over F\,b --- we take \overline {\mathcal {D}} in the image of F

html:div.style: flex: 1; min-width: 0
border-left: 4px solid var(--accent); background: var(--bg-subtle, rgba(0,0,0,0.03)); padding: 0.7em 1em; margin: 0.8em 0; border-radius: 2px
color: var(--accent); font-variant: small-caps; letter-spacing: 0.12em; font-size: 0.85em; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.3em

html:div.html:div: Reindexing preserves fibrations and preserves vertical universal properties

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Originally, proving canonicity meant building a displayed cartesian category directly over \mathbf {Syntax}_{\Sigma ,\times }. We have reduced that to:

html:ol.html:li: Pick a category \mathcal {C} and a functor F : \mathbf {Syntax}_{\Sigma ,\times } \to \mathcal {C}
Build a vertical cartesian category \overline {\mathcal {D}} over \mathcal {C}
Reindex along F to get a vertical cartesian fibration F^{*}\overline {\mathcal {D}} over \mathbf {Syntax}_{\Sigma ,\times }
Apply vertical-to-displayed to get a displayed cartesian category over \mathbf {Syntax}_{\Sigma ,\times }
Use the freeness of \mathbf {Syntax}_{\Sigma ,\times } to get the desired section

html:div.style: border-left: 4px solid var(--accent); background: var(--bg-subtle, rgba(0,0,0,0.03)); padding: 0.7em 1em; margin: 0.8em 0; border-radius: 2px
color: var(--accent); font-variant: small-caps; letter-spacing: 0.12em; font-size: 0.85em; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.3em

html:div.html:div: Take \mathcal {C} = \mathbf {Set} and \overline {\mathcal {\mathbf {Set}}} the displayed category whose objects over a set X are families X \to \mathbf {Set}. The functor G : \mathbf {Syntax}_{\Sigma ,\times } \to \mathbf {Set} is global sections, sending a type A to its set of closed terms \{M \mid \cdot \vdash M : A\}.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Concretely proving \overline {\mathcal {\mathbf {Set}}} is vertically cartesian (closed) involves chasing a lot of transports. They are an annoying matter of coherence, but we can largely paper over them with fillers

html:div.html:p: For a goal that has 6 nested transports/reinds, a reasonably short chain of reind-fillers does the job

html:pre.html:code: SETᴰ.rectifyOut $ SETᴰ.reind-filler⁻ _ ∙ SETᴰ.congᴰ (λ (u : uTy) z zᴰ → f z (u z zᴰ)) (funExt₂ λ z zᴰ → ΣPathP ((funExt₂⁻ (SETᴰ.rectifyOut $ SETᴰ.reind-filler⁻ _) z zᴰ) , funExt₂⁻ (SETᴰ.rectifyOut $ SETᴰ.reind-filler⁻ _ ∙ SETᴰ.reind-filler⁻ _ ∙ SETᴰ.reind-filler⁻ _ ∙ SETᴰ.reind-filler⁻ _) z zᴰ)) where g*Xᴰ = isFibrationSETᴰ._*_ {x = Z} g Xᴰ uTy = (z : ⟨ Z ⟩) → (⟨ Zᴰ z ⟩ × ⟨ Xᴰ (g z) ⟩) → ⟨ Zᴰ z ⟩ × ⟨ g*Xᴰ z ⟩

html:div.html:p: However, this becomes a performance bottleneck for Agda typechecking. Tractable for displayed category of families of sets; intractably slow for displayed category of displayed presheaves

html:div.style: border-left: 4px solid var(--accent); background: var(--bg-subtle, rgba(0,0,0,0.03)); padding: 0.7em 1em; margin: 0.8em 0; border-radius: 2px
color: var(--accent); font-variant: small-caps; letter-spacing: 0.12em; font-size: 0.85em; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.3em

html:div.html:div: Many of these transports are over refl. For the Cubical Path type, \mathsf {transport}\,\mathsf {refl} does not reduce. For an inductive equality \mathsf {Eq}, it does reduce definitionally

html:div.html:p: We use \mathsf {Eq} complementarily alongside \mathsf {Path} to keep these chains tractable

html:div.style: border-left: 4px solid var(--accent); background: var(--bg-subtle, rgba(0,0,0,0.03)); padding: 0.7em 1em; margin: 0.8em 0; border-radius: 2px
color: var(--accent); font-variant: small-caps; letter-spacing: 0.12em; font-size: 0.85em; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.3em

html:div.html:div: The trick only works because the equalities we transport over really are \mathsf {Eq}.\mathsf {refl} --- and this only holds because \mathbf {Set} (and our category of presheaves) is strict

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Once the framework is in place, we can plug and play to derive new results

html:ul.html:li: Canonicity for more theories --- products, sums, exponentials
Conservativity for extensions of theories --- i.e. products + functions over products
Coherence for monoidal categories
Canonicity for a guarded type theory

html:div.style: border-left: 4px solid var(--accent); background: var(--bg-subtle, rgba(0,0,0,0.03)); padding: 0.7em 1em; margin: 0.8em 0; border-radius: 2px
color: var(--accent); font-variant: small-caps; letter-spacing: 0.12em; font-size: 0.85em; font-weight: 600; margin-bottom: 0.3em

html:ul.html:li: Categories with families for dependent type theory
Effectful languages, substructual languages
Languages with equational axioms in their signatures --- e.g. encoding recursors for inductive types internally to the object language
Displayifying more categorical structures --- like initial algebras as different route to inductives

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Other experimental directions we're exploring with the library

html:ul.html:li: Locally small category theory — level-polymorphic universal properties via categorical structures displayed over a category of levels
Compositional metatheory for effectful languages and call-by-push-value
Logical relations for guarded type theories
(Preliminarily) 2-category theory — bicategories, double categories, virtual equipments, etc.
Experiments on doing category theory with more definitonal equalities in the proof assistant: Yoneda strictification of categories, thickening types by adding redundant data

Convenient bifunctor encodings — naive bifunctors aren't definitionally well-behaved when acting by the identity in one component and a nontrivial morphism in the other; we experiment with alternatives that bridge this gap

fr:mainmatter.html:p: (Displayed) category theory is an effective foundation for reusable, compositional mechanizinization of programming language semantics
Abstract constructions can be reused across many applications, leaving concrete metatheorems as corollaries to a small number of properties for a semantic domain

Cubical Agda is mostly suited towards hosting these constructions, but slow typechecking performance can halt formalization progress. Transport hell is not just tedium for a developer; it is also a bottleneck
